title: Body Systems in Animals
seo_title: Grade 5 Science: Body Systems in Animals Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: The human body has organ systems (digestive, skeletal and muscular, nervous, respiratory, circulatory) that work together; healthy habits keep them working well. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 5, Quarter 2: Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Living Things): the digestive system, bones, muscles and nerves, the respiratory system, the circulatory system and systems working together. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Organ systems work together to keep you alive.
key_sub: Lungs take in oxygen; the heart pumps it around the body.
body_html:
How to think about it

The digestive system (mouth, osophagus, stomach, intestines) breaks food down so nutrients can enter the blood. The musculoskeletal system (bones and muscles) supports and moves the body. The respiratory system (lungs, diaphragm) brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. The circulatory system (heart, blood vessels) carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.

Systems work together: during exercise you breathe faster and your heart beats faster to deliver more oxygen to your muscles.

Example

Where is most food absorbed into the blood?

A long, folded tube after the stomach

Answer: the small intestine

Example

Which muscle helps you breathe in?

It is under the lungs.

Answer: the diaphragm

Common mistakes

  • Thinking food goes straight from the stomach into the blood.
  • Thinking the lungs pump blood.
  • Forgetting that muscles can only pull, not push.

faq.q: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
faq.a: Your muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps blood faster.

faq.q: How are bones and muscles a machine?
faq.a: Bones act as levers and muscles pull on them at the joints.

items.q: Food leaves the small intestine. Where does it go next?
items.e: mouth → gullet → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.

items.q: What is an organ?
c: a body part made of tissues that does a special job
a type of blood vessel only
items.e: The heart, lungs and stomach are organs.

items.q: Food leaves the stomach. Where does it go next?
items.e: mouth → gullet → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.

items.q: Food reaches the small intestine. Where has it just come from?
items.e: mouth → gullet → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.

items.q:
In which part of the digestive system does this happen?
Food stays here for a few hours and is partly digested.
items.e: Food stays here for a few hours and is partly digested.

items.q:
In which part of the digestive system does this happen?
Undigested food is stored here until it leaves the body.
items.e: Undigested food is stored here until it leaves the body.

items.q:
In which part of the digestive system does this happen?
Digested food is absorbed into the blood here.
items.e: Digested food is absorbed into the blood here.

items.q:
In which part of the digestive system does this happen?
It churns food and mixes it with digestive juices.
items.e: It churns food and mixes it with digestive juices.

items.q: Food leaves the mouth. Where does it go next?
items.e: mouth → gullet → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.

items.q: Which organ does the brain work with to let you see?
items.e: Eyes send signals to the brain.

items.q: What does the liver make that helps digest fats?
items.e: Bile breaks fat into small drops.

items.q:
In which part of the digestive system does this happen?
Teeth chew food into smaller pieces and saliva makes it soft.
items.e: Teeth chew food into smaller pieces and saliva makes it soft.

items.q: Why do we need fiber in our food?
c: It helps us see in the dark.
It helps food move through the intestines.
items.e: Fiber is found in vegetables and whole grains.

items.q: What does the ribs (rib cage) do?
c: It lets the arm lift and move.
It protects the spinal cord and holds the body upright.
It protect the heart and lungs.
items.e: Many bones protect soft organs.

items.q: What does the kneecap do?
c: It holds the bottom teeth and lets us chew.
It protect the heart and lungs.
It lets the arm lift and move.
items.e: Many bones protect soft organs.

items.q: Which bone is the longest bone and helps us stand and walk?
items.e: Match the bone to its job.

items.q: A helmet of bone covers the brain. Which job of the skeleton is this?
items.e: The skeleton supports, protects and helps us move.

items.q: The knee joint lets the leg bend when we kick a ball. Which job of the skeleton is this?
items.e: The skeleton supports, protects and helps us move.

items.q: What joins muscles to bones?
items.e: Muscles pull bones by contracting. They work in pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

items.q: What happens to muscles that are exercised often?
items.e: Muscles pull bones by contracting. They work in pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

items.q: Which organ is a muscle that never stops working?
items.e: Muscles pull bones by contracting. They work in pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

items.q: The spine surrounds the spinal cord. Which job of the skeleton is this?
items.e: The skeleton supports, protects and helps us move.

items.q: Which bone protects the knee joint?
items.e: Match the bone to its job.

items.q: When you bend your arm, what does your biceps (front of the upper arm) do?
c: It contracts (gets shorter) and pulls the lower arm up.
items.e: Muscles pull bones by contracting. They work in pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

items.q: Dennis sees a car coming. Which sense organ takes in this information?
items.e: This information is taken in by the eyes (sight).

items.q: When you kick a ball, the muscle at the front of your thigh contracts. What does it do?
c: It pulls the lower leg forwards to straighten the knee.
items.e: Muscles pull bones by contracting. They work in pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

items.q: Mae smells smoke. Which sense organ takes in this information?
items.e: This information is taken in by the nose (smell).

items.q: Christian hears a dog growl. Which sense organ takes in this information?
items.e: This information is taken in by the ears (hearing).

items.q: Where in the body is the humerus?
items.e: Learn the main bones and where they are.

items.q: When you straighten your arm, what does your triceps (back of the upper arm) do?
c: It contracts and pulls the lower arm straight.
items.e: Muscles pull bones by contracting. They work in pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

items.q: Kristine tastes a bitter berry. Which sense organ takes in this information?
items.e: This information is taken in by the tongue (taste).

items.q: The spine keeps us upright. Which job of the skeleton is this?
items.e: The skeleton supports, protects and helps us move.

items.q: What does a muscle do when it contracts?
c: It gets shorter and fatter and pulls on a bone.
It lets go of the bone.
It gets longer and pushes a bone.
items.e: Muscles pull bones by contracting. They work in pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

items.q: When you breathe in, what happens to the pressure inside the chest?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through a bronchus. Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through the trachea (windpipe). Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: When you breathe out, what happens to the ribcage?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
items.e: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood.

items.q: When you breathe out, what happens to the intercostal muscles?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: What is the job of cilia?
c: Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.
Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: When you breathe out, what happens to the diaphragm?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: What is the job of the bronchioles?
c: Bones that protect the lungs and heart.
A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: What is the job of the trachea (windpipe)?
c: Two tubes that carry air from the trachea into each lung.
Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: When you breathe in, what happens to the intercostal muscles?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: Which gas do we breathe out more of than we breathe in?
items.e: Cells make carbon dioxide as waste.

items.q: When you breathe in, what happens to the volume of the chest?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: Which organ systems work together to get oxygen to your muscles?
items.e: Lungs take in oxygen; blood carries it.

items.q: When you breathe out, what happens to the volume of the chest?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Two tubes that carry air from the trachea into each lung.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: What is the job of the ribs?
c: Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Bones that protect the lungs and heart.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through the nose or mouth. Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: How does smoking harm the respiratory system?
c: It makes the lungs bigger and healthier.
It damages the lungs so they take in less oxygen.
items.e: Smoke damages the air sacs.

items.q: Which part carries blood to and from all parts of the body?
items.e: The blood vessels carry blood to and from all parts of the body.

items.q: Which part pumps blood around the body?
items.e: The heart pumps blood around the body.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: carrying blood away from the heart?
items.e: Arteries: carrying blood away from the heart.

items.q: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
c: Your muscles need more oxygen, so blood must flow faster.
items.e: Exercise increases heart rate.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: carrying nutrients, water and waste as a liquid?
items.e: Plasma: carrying nutrients, water and waste as a liquid.

items.q: What is the main job of arteries?
c: carrying blood away from the heart
carrying blood back to the heart
giving the blood oxygen and taking away carbon dioxide
items.e: Arteries: carrying blood away from the heart.

items.q: Which part takes in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide?
items.e: The lungs take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

items.q: Blood leaves the right side of the heart. Where does it go next?
c: the left side of the heart
items.e: Body → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → body.

items.q: Blood arrives at the right side of the heart. Where has it just come from?
c: the left side of the heart
items.e: Body → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → body.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: carrying blood back to the heart?
items.e: Veins: carrying blood back to the heart.

items.q: What is the function of the blood vessels?
c: Carries oxygen, digested food and water to the cells.
Take in oxygen dissolved in water for fish.
Carry blood to and from all parts of the body.
Take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
items.e: The blood vessels carry blood to and from all parts of the body.

items.q: What is the main job of capillaries?
c: helping blood clot to stop bleeding
letting oxygen and nutrients pass into the cells
carrying blood back to the heart
items.e: Capillaries: letting oxygen and nutrients pass into the cells.

items.q: What path does air take into the lungs?
c: nose or mouth → windpipe (trachea) → bronchi → lungs
items.e: Air travels down the windpipe.

items.q: Where does oxygen pass into the blood?
items.e: Tiny air sacs in the lungs pass oxygen to the blood.

items.q: Which part lets gases enter and leave a plant?
items.e: The tiny openings on leaves let gases enter and leave a plant.

items.q: What does an asthma inhaler do?
c: It opens up the airways so air can flow more easily.
items.e: Medical technology helps people breathe.

items.q: What is the function of the tiny openings on leaves?
c: Let gases enter and leave a plant.
Carries oxygen, digested food and water to the cells.
Are where oxygen passes into the blood.
Take in oxygen dissolved in water for fish.
items.e: The tiny openings on leaves let gases enter and leave a plant.

items.q: What is the function of the heart?
c: Carries oxygen, digested food and water to the cells.
Are where oxygen passes into the blood.
Carry blood to and from all parts of the body.
items.e: The heart pumps blood around the body.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: fighting germs that cause disease?
items.e: White blood cells: fighting germs that cause disease.

items.q: What is the function of the lungs?
c: Take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
Carries air from the nose to the lungs.
Let gases enter and leave a plant.
Are where oxygen passes into the blood.
items.e: The lungs take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

items.q: Air we breathe in passes through the nose. Where does it go next?
items.e: nose → windpipe → lungs → air sacs.

items.q: Air reaches the windpipe. Where did it come from just before?
items.e: nose → windpipe → lungs → air sacs.

items.q: Which substance does the blood carry from all parts of the body to the lungs?
items.e: The blood carries oxygen, digested food and water to the cells, and carbon dioxide to the lungs.

items.q: What do blood vessels called arteries do?
c: carry blood toward the heart only
carry blood away from the heart
items.e: Arteries carry blood away; veins bring it back.

items.q: The blood carries water. In which direction?
c: from the intestines to all parts of the body
from the lungs to all parts of the body
from the small intestine to all parts of the body
from all parts of the body to the lungs
items.e: The blood transports substances around the body.

items.q: Which gas does the body need from the air?
items.e: Cells use oxygen to release energy from food.

items.q: Is blood in the right side of the heart rich in oxygen or low in oxygen?
c: it has no oxygen at all
items.e: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives it to the body's cells.

items.q: The blood carries oxygen. In which direction?
c: from the intestines to all parts of the body
from all parts of the body to the lungs
from the small intestine to all parts of the body
from the lungs to all parts of the body
items.e: The blood transports substances around the body.

items.q: Air we breathe in passes through the lungs. Where does it go next?
items.e: nose → windpipe → lungs → air sacs.

items.q: Is blood leaving the lungs rich in oxygen or low in oxygen?
c: it has no oxygen at all
items.e: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives it to the body's cells.

items.q: Where does oxygen pass into the blood?
c: in the air sacs of the lungs
items.e: The air sacs have very thin walls.

items.q: The blood carries digested food. In which direction?
c: from all parts of the body to the lungs
from the small intestine to all parts of the body
from the intestines to all parts of the body
from the lungs to all parts of the body
items.e: The blood transports substances around the body.

items.q: Is blood in the arteries going to the leg muscles rich in oxygen or low in oxygen?
c: it has no oxygen at all
items.e: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives it to the body's cells.

items.q: What do veins do?
c: carry blood away from the heart
carry blood back to the heart
items.e: Veins return blood to the heart.

items.q: What is the job of the diaphragm?
c: It moves down to help pull air into the lungs.
items.e: The diaphragm is a muscle under the lungs.

items.q: What is the pulse?
c: the beat felt at the wrist or neck when the heart pumps blood
items.e: Each pulse beat matches one heartbeat.

items.q: Is blood leaving a hard-working muscle rich in oxygen or low in oxygen?
c: it has no oxygen at all
items.e: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives it to the body's cells.

items.q: Which gas does the body get rid of when we breathe out?
items.e: Carbon dioxide is a waste gas.

items.q: Which substance does the blood carry from the intestines to all parts of the body?
items.e: The blood carries oxygen, digested food and water to the cells, and carbon dioxide to the lungs.

items.q: Air we breathe in passes through the windpipe. Where does it go next?
items.e: nose → windpipe → lungs → air sacs.
